text: Hello and welcome to the latest AFI podcast, taking you inside the key trends shaping
the $5 trillion plus global hedge fund industry. My name is Will Wainwright.
This week we have a special interview with Paul Glazer, founder of New York hedge fund
firm Glazer Capital, founded in 1999 which now runs about $2.5 billion. The firm started
with a merge arbitrage strategy and has since expanded to include special purpose acquisitions
or SPACs and a convertible bonds strategy. In its 27 year history, the firm has never
had a down year. Glazer Capital now has a 50 person team working on its strategies which
makes it one of the largest teams dedicated to merger arbitrage on Wall Street.
Join leaders of the global hedge fund industry at the AFI Innovation Summit coming to May
this October. If you would like to take part as a delegate, speaker or sponsor at this exclusive
gathering which will bring together senior operational staff including COOs, CTOs and heads
of ops from global billion dollar plus hedge funds, please message me on LinkedIn or email
will at alternativefundinsight.com. It is set to be a fantastic day of discussion,
networking and best practice benchmarking in the heart of Mayfair. Thursday 8th October and the
initial agenda is online now. Head to alternativefundinsight.com slash events for more information.
This podcast is brought to you in association with SITCO, the leading asset servicer with over
two trillion dollars of assets under administration and the top hedge fund administrator on the AFI
250 research ranking. SITCO acts as a true partner to its clients, dedicated to developing rich
long term relationships through gold standard services and industry leading technology.
Head to SITCO.com for more information. Now to the interview. Thank you for joining me on the AFI
podcast today. It's great to be speaking to you live from New York City. Perhaps we could kick
off with a brief overview of Glazer Capital and your thoughts on the firm's evolution and where
it is today. The firm I started in 1999 with one person and a million dollars under management and
after 27 years of investing, we have 2.8 billion dollars, nearly 50 employees.
And we've also evolved from just merger arbitrage to now being active in SPAC arbitrage,
convertible arbitrage, and event driven fixed income. The goal has always been to produce
absolute returns without having market correlation. And we have a history of success with getting
through the great financial crisis, COVID, and most recently the tariff tantrum and the Middle
East conflicts and still having happy investors. Well, that is a very long lifespan in the context
of the global hedge fund industry. But I'd like to start by just going back to the beginning.
You started Glazer Capital after your sales side career. What was the initial deal that
really crystallized your philosophy and led to that decision? Right. So the inspiration I would
like to say for starting Glazer Capital really happened in 1998. After being on the sell side for
nine years, I was beginning to feel a little bit like my position as an institutional equity salesman
was more psychologist rather than a financial advisor. I had one particular client
who I would talk to him every day at that time about office devote staples. And that was really
a situation that I thought would be very hard to handicap. And I thought that it was really
not worthwhile to invest in such a position in that I could start a firm that would avoid
that type of thing. The problem with the office devote staples deal was that they were the two
largest office super store chains in the United States at that time. And that in itself
was a very interesting anti-trust question. Would you call office super stores a national
market or is it a series of local markets? You could buy your office supplies from a lot of
local suppliers that were regional chains. But if you wanted to buy in all 50 states,
you basically had only the two choices of office devote staples. So it was a real
question for the regulators. Is this a national market or a local market? So one day I was talking
with this investor and he said, well, you know, Paul, what would you do? You know, would you be
longer short this position? And I said, you know what, neither. I would sit this one out. I don't
know, you know, which way it's going to go. The regulator, you know, I may be right and the regulator
may be wrong, but he's the one who still has the power. I said, I would sit it out. You could sit
it out also. And at that point, my client said, what do you mean I could sit this out? I get paid
to make these decisions. And at that point, I recognized that he had a lot of ego invested.
There's a lot of ego and people trying to be right and trying to figure out questions that
require clairvoyance. Basically, you can't figure out what's going on in the head of the regulator.
And I thought there could be a better merger arbitrage fund that I could start that would
avoid situations like that and really just focus on the lower risk deals. And even though they had
smaller spreads, they still had attractive spreads and it still had produced a very
attractive risk adjusted rate of return. And that's been borne out over the past 27 years.
Yeah. And so in terms of your strategy range, you know, merger arbitrage is still very,
very much a core strategy. There's been some moves into the SPAC market and invertibles.
Maybe you could just paint a picture of what Glazer is doing now.
Sure. So we were almost 100% merger arbitrage up until the great financial crisis.
At that point, we learned about the opportunity in SPACs. SPACs went to a discount to cash and
trust, a significant discount anywhere from 5% to 10% or sometimes even more. So it was literally
buying dollar bills for 90 cents. And we got into the SPAC business in a pretty significant way in
2009. And we've been in it ever since, ever since then. It's an attractive low risk arbitrage type
of situation with upside optionality because the SPAC sometimes announced very attractive deals
and they go to big premiums over their cash and trust. And that can be a bit of a home run.
The next area we got into in a significant way was a bent driven fixed income, also during
the great financial crisis. Bons were close to maturity or bonds that were being redeemed or
called or tendered for. That became an interesting area during the great financial crisis and we've
been active there ever since. And in the past two plus years, we've gotten involved in convertible
arbitrage, also in a way that its goal is to produce absolute returns. And it's a bit of a
counterbalance to merger arbitrage because merger arbitrage spreads tend to widen out during times
of volatility or times when the market goes down. But convertible arbitrage can do well
during those periods. And then we've actually seen that in the past couple of years that we've had
this book. When the ball increases or the market goes down a lot, the fix goes up, then you can
have an increase in valuation in convertible arbitrage. So those are the four main strategies
that we have right now. Yeah. And how does the current set of opportunities
compare when you look back through Glazer's 27 year history? How would you frame the market
situation at the moment for what you do day to day? Right. It's really very good right now,
particularly in all of our strategies. Merger arbitrage being our largest strategy,
most important one because it is our largest strategy, is in particular enjoying a rejuvenation
over the past year and a half since Donald Trump has been in office. I just want to preface the
remark by saying that there's always activity in M&A and there's always opportunities in
Merger arbitrage. There are better times and worse times. So really, we have enjoyed an improvement
since the new administration came in just because the regulatory regime has become
much more friendly towards business. I mean, you had a new head of the FTC's antitrust effort
that came in with Donald Trump and he said explicitly, if there's a problem with the deal
from antitrust, we're going to try to block it. But if there isn't, we're going to get out of the
way and let business happen using the phrase get out of the way. That's a phrase that I don't think
we ever heard under the previous administration of Joe Biden or certainly during the Obama
administration either. That has created more deal activity and there have been more $10
billion plus deals in the first half of 2026 than we've had in any other six month period since
Bloomberg has been keeping records. So that activity really, it does a couple of things,
that it increases our opportunity set and allows us to be more fully invested. It allows us to be
more diversified because if any particular deal runs into issues, we have more diversification,
which I think I believe smooths out our returns. And the bigger deals tend to have wider spreads
just because they're so big. Arbs really can't control the spread, which is what happens when
you have a smaller deal. The big deal, you get a lot of fundamental sellers, particularly in a
downed day in the market and the spread will widen and that creates an opportunity for us.
So we're arbitrage is really in a good spot right now.
That's in the US. We've had this deregulatory drive as you mentioned, which has boosted the
environment. It would be good to get your thoughts internationally starting with
Europe and the UK. Do you see opportunities in those regions too?
Yeah, Europe has taken the cue from the United States and we have seen the UK in particular
appointed a new head of the CMA, the Competitions and Markets Authority,
the Antitrust Regulatory in the UK, who was the former head of Amazon UK.
So that's definitely a person who's going to be more sympathetic and friendlier towards the
business community. And we have heard anecdotally in the UK and in Europe that they would like
to produce and to help their, quote, national champions, their big companies as a way of competing
with US companies, which are in a sense have the shackles taken off in the US.
So that has unleashed more activity also in Europe and I believe there's lower risk.
And in response to this, we created a London office two years ago, which has really been
very helpful. You also have greater activity in Japan. We started investing there a year ago for
the very first time. Japan has changed its policy. They are now looking for greater business efficiency
rather than just lifetime employment and other social goals of businesses. They want to see
greater efficiency because they have a population, their population is declining. So they really
need to do this and greater efficiency oftentimes means more mergers and acquisitions of smaller
companies being merged together, bigger companies buying smaller companies. That's been a
profitable area that we've looked that we've gotten active in the past year.
Yeah, it's really interesting. The Japanese opportunity has been quite a growing theme
in the hedge fund world over the past few years. And you've obviously seen an angle there.
Okay, well, that's a great overview of the M&A and the merger arbitrage space. It remains your core
strategy, your bread and butter. But I do want to talk a bit more about SPACs and convertibles too.
So let's start with SPACs. You know, very, very interesting market. It's had its ups and downs,
notably in 2021. It would be good to get your thoughts on what makes this cycle different
and what is the opportunity set going forward? Right. So as I said, we had been invested in
those successfully since 2009. And our success and our size of our exposure and investment in
SPACs is really determined by how big this SPAC market is, how many SPACs are outstanding. So
you had a boom in SPAC IBOs in 2020 and in 2021. And that was all started because some SPACs, when
they announced deals back in 2019 and 2020, took off. They had very interesting situations. They
were getting into electric cars and electric car batteries and all types of new technology, whatever
was on the investment public's shortlist or hot list at that time. SPACs were merging with those
and they were just doing great. A lot of those companies, unfortunately, were not great companies
and investors ended up losing money. So you had a dearth of IBOs, 2022, 23, 24. Things kind of came
really settled down very quickly. We saw a pickup, again, well, last year, 2025, with a lot more
IBOs. And this year, we're on pace to have more IBOs than we've had since 2021. So that's been
very good for us. A lot of the SPACs are trading at attractive levels, relative to their cash and
trust. And you've had this year, some deals get announced where they've gone to in 2020.
Where they've gone to premiums to their cash and trust. I don't think we're going to go back to
what we saw in 2020 or 2021. But it doesn't take very many of those to really make this
a profitable area. And even without any of those, it's still a profitable investment just because
of the carry aspect of owning the SPACs. And just to dive into that a bit more deeply, how do you
size exposure and manage the concentration when you're picking out these deals?
Yeah. So with SPACs, they generally are of limited size that can be $200-$300 million
in market capitalization. So we have to limit ourselves to 9.9% usually, not always,
but oftentimes. So that'll be a $20-$30 million position. And that's how we get limited in the
SPACs. That's relatively easy. The risk control is very easy in SPACs because the risk is very,
very low, in my opinion, comes to SPAC investing, at least the way that we do it,
without trying to figure out what are going to be the new businesses that they're launching.
In merger arbitrage, we limit the position sizes based on basically a risk budget per position.
So we try to have a finite amount of risk in every single position. And if the more confident
we are in the success of the deal going through, the bigger our budget, our risk budget will be
for that position. Like I said, we have an advantage by having so many different positions.
I believe that our merger arbitrage team is the largest merger arbitrage team in existence.
And with that, it allows us to re-invest in 100 deals or more at any given time.
And that diversification, I think A, gives us a bigger opportunity set and allows more
profit opportunities. And B, I think reduces the overall volatility because if any given
position goes wrong, then you have 99 other positions that hopefully are not going wrong.
So that's I think point value added for our investment strategy.
Yeah, that's such an interesting point. And I just want to pick up on that before turning
to convertibles. You've been focused on merger arbitrage. It's interesting in the last few years,
we've had the growth of the PodShop model. And these firms have brought in pods focused on
various strategies, including merger arbitrage when there have been opportunities. What do you
make of that market dynamic and the role of the PodShops, the multistrats, compared to the single
managers? It's a good question. Well, we are very aware of the PodShop model and they,
you know, any individual being multi-strat will have more merger arbitrage orders than
glazed capital halves, but they're in different pockets. So you can run into concentration
issues. I think that they may all be looking at the same deals, the same issues with them and that
because they have to be invested and because the way their incentives are set up, it can create
some volatility in the market. It's a double-edged sword in that A, they tend to have a lot of money
and that can compress spreads, but B, it can oftentimes be on a hair trigger and that can
make spreads volatile and that can be helpful for us and allow us to take advantage of those
situations when they arise. Yeah, really interesting to get your take on that. And
finally, let's just turn now to convertibles in terms of the strategy spread.
Really interesting time in this space. Convertible issuance just hit a monthly record.
So what do you think is driving that? What do you make of the quality of issuance in this cycle
and maybe a couple of examples? Sure, convertible arbitrage has really evolved
since my start in this business a long time ago. It used to be second-tier companies,
lower credit quality companies who could not issue regular debt or they could get cheaper
interest rates if they issued convertible debt. Now you've had giant companies like DoorDash
and OnSemiconductor or Sienna and these are 30, 50 plus billion-dollar market cap companies
with quasi-investment grade companies issuing convertible debt. So that's very, very good
for our strategy, our style of convertible arbitrage investing. We like to avoid credit
questions. So we're focusing on just high-credit quality names. So that
could be a problem because oftentimes a high-credit quality names don't have a lot of volatility
in their equity, which is not good for being able to trade around these positions. But
now you have these giant tech companies that have a great deal of volatility in their equity.
So they really are very right for trading around and basically collecting the gamma that you get
by being long the convertible and short the equity. So that puts us in a good position of
buying the stock when it goes down and selling the stock when it goes up. All we need is the
volatility. We don't know which of the names are going to do it, but with the portfolio of names
and tech names that we own that are the issuers, it's worked out pretty well for the past couple
of years that we've been in this strategy. You also have a benefit in convertible bonds that
you've had a very, very active issuance market. As you said, you had a recent monthly record of
issuance on track, I believe, for a record year of issuance in 2006. Generally, convertible bonds
are issued at attractive levels. You can usually make money right out of the gate. That's an
important source of returns for us and for most people who do a group of partners. The activity
has really been fantastic. Just yesterday, there were four new issues in the market. It's really a
robust market. I don't see that changing between now and the end of the year.
With issuance at such a high level, what does that mean for capacity going forward?
It's good for our capacity. Right now, given the robustness of the M&A market and
SPAC new issuance in the size of that market and convertible market, we are looking at more
opportunities than we have capital for at the moment. We have closed twice in our history over
the past 27 years when the opportunity set wasn't there. Staffing, I think, wasn't there to take
on more capital, but we are near 50 employees and a very robust opportunity set in all of our
core strategies. The capacity is looking pretty good right now.
Having those two in position, having the opportunity set and the infrastructure
is both very important parts to have in place, given the changes in global politics and society
and markets since you started the firm. What is it? Is there something in particular that keeps
you up at night more than it used to now? No, it's a short answer. Actually, I think our strategy
has become lower risk than it was when I started in 1999. After the great financial crisis, deals
have more solid financing on them. That's one risk that we used to think about a lot. Particularly
back when I was a salesman, there were deals that were subject to financing. That really doesn't
happen anymore. The deals really all have very solid financing. I believe the investment banks
have become more conservative in their lending post-financial crisis. That's one risk that's
really off the table. Regulatory risk was always there. That's just reading the regulators and
listening to what they say and to see how they enforce what they're supposed to enforce. That
hasn't really changed. You have, I think, fewer deals where you have buyer votes. There were more
mergers of equals or type of things that required a buyer shareholder vote, which can tend to be
riskier. We have fewer situations like that. We tend to avoid those situations. You had periods
of other risks like the bankruptcies in the early 2000s of WorldCom and Enron and options
backdating scandals. I think, in a sense, the accounting has gotten better. The accountants
and the auditors have gotten better. I think there's less fraud risk today than there may have been
25 years ago. The backdrop, I think, is lower risk. We still have to approach this
with the humility to know what you know and know what you don't know and be willing to admit that
you don't know it and you can't find out it. It's a sound of trouble.
I just want to ask a couple of final questions about culture. You've been hiring staff and
expanding this decade. You've been developing talent. I'd be interested to hear your approach to
all of that. Also, in particular, I believe you have a no swearing policy in the office.
That definitely contrasts with some other hedge funds I've spoken to.
Thank you for asking. I'm actually very proud of our no foul language policy. I think it creates
a much more collaborative environment and the opposite of a toxic workplace. The senior people
are people that I have known a long time, even though one of our senior people was just hired
two and a half years ago. It's somebody we've known for more than 10 years.
We have really assembled a top tier team of people that I have a good history with who fit
very well without culture. On the investment side, the rest of the firm also has very good
longevity in our operations and investor relations side. We've developed a technology team that now
has six people. Five years ago, it had zero people. We dedicate a lot of resources towards
automating parts of our investing research process and making our operations much more
efficient now that we have four main strategies and many different line items on our portfolio.
So I'm proud of what we've built here. I think that we've created a great place to work and I
think that that comes through and helps with the collaborative nature of how we're producing our
returns. How do you augment the human culture and that collaboration with all of the technology and
AI tools that are now available? How are you implementing those?
Right. The AI is really being used as an adjunct and an efficiency tool. So our research analysts
are more efficient than they were two years ago, let's say, or even a year ago, just because they
have good AI tools that can analyze a merger agreement very quickly. We put a lot of effort into
getting that right. We are able to do the same thing on the operations side as well.
That's also made our people more efficient. So I don't foresee us. AI decreasing our head count,
but I do have seen it and I can predict. I predict that I will continue to see it and
it will make us faster and better at what we're doing going forward, hopefully.
Good stuff, Paul. Well, I will leave it there. Thank you for joining me today
and all the best for the rest of 2026. Well, thank you very much. Thanks.
Thank you to Paul Glazer for those insights and we will see you next time on the AFI podcast.
